lede: Components can be joined in one loop or on separate branches. Each way has a rule for the current and a rule for the voltage, and together the four rules let you fill in any meter reading a question leaves blank.
can: Tell a series circuit from a parallel one by tracing the route the current takes
Use the series rules and the parallel rules to find any missing meter reading
Share a current between two unequal parallel branches

md: Take one cell and two lamps. In one loop, pull a lamp out and the other goes dark; on separate branches, it stays lit. This topic is that difference, and one fact beneath it: charge is never used up going round.

md: First decide which circuit you have: follow the route from the cell back to the cell. One route through every component in turn is **series**. A route that splits at a **junction** into branches and joins again is **parallel**.
**On the figure.** The top arrows pass both lamps in turn. The bottom arrows split at a junction dot, one path per lamp, and meet again. Judge by the route, not the layout.

prompt: A cell, a switch and two lamps are joined so that the current leaving the cell reaches a junction and can pass through either lamp before the two paths meet again. Which kind of circuit is this?
options: parallel: the route splits at a junction and joins again
series: there is one route round the loop
neither, because the circuit contains a switch
answer: parallel: the route splits at a junction and joins again
explain: Follow the route the way the arrows do on the figure. Here it reaches a junction and splits, one lamp on each path, then joins again: that is parallel. In series there would be one path through both lamps in turn, with no choice. A switch does not change the kind of circuit; it only opens or closes the route it sits in. The answer is parallel.

caption: Three ammeters in one loop, before, between and after the resistors: the same reading at every point.

md: A series circuit is one loop, so the charge passing the first component has nowhere else to go: it passes the second too. **The current is the same at every point.** A component takes energy from the charge, not the charge itself.

title: Why the current is not used up
md: Current is the charge passing a point each second. Charge cannot pile up in a wire or vanish inside a component, so whatever flows into a component flows out of it.
**Read the figure.** 0.30 A before the 12 Ω resistor, 0.30 A between, 0.30 A after the 18 Ω resistor. Know one reading in a series loop and you know them all.

prompt: In a series circuit one ammeter sits just before a lamp and another just after it. The first reads 0.15 A. What does the second read, in amps?
explain: A series circuit is one loop, and a lamp takes energy from the charge, not charge from the current. So the same current flows in and out of the lamp, just as the three ammeters on the figure all read the same. The second ammeter reads 0.15 A.

caption: A voltmeter across each resistor: the two readings add up to the supply voltage.

md: Voltage measures the energy each unit of charge carries. The supply gives the charge its energy once, and the components in the loop take that energy in turn. So **in series, the voltages across the components add up to the supply voltage**: the supply is shared out, and the larger resistance takes the larger share.

**Read the figure.** Across the 12 Ω resistor 3.6 V; across the 18 Ω resistor 5.4 V. Add them: 3.6 + 5.4 = 9.0 V, the supply. So a missing voltage is the supply take away the readings you already have.

prompt: Two components are in series with a 4.5 V supply. The voltmeter across the first component reads 1.5 V. What does a voltmeter across the second component read, in volts?
explain: In series the supply is shared out along the loop, so the two readings must add up to the supply, as 3.6 V and 5.4 V did on the figure. The second reading is 4.5 − 1.5 = 3.0 V. Giving it the whole 4.5 V would be the parallel rule used on a series circuit.

caption: Two different resistors on two branches, and both voltmeters read the supply voltage.

md: Each branch of a parallel circuit is joined straight across the supply, one end to each terminal. So **in parallel, the voltage across every branch is the supply voltage**, whatever is on the branch. That is why every lamp in a house has the full mains voltage across it, however many others are switched on.

**Read the figure.** A 6.0 V supply, a 20 Ω resistor on one branch and a 30 Ω resistor on the other. Both voltmeters read 6.0 V. Different resistances, the same voltage: nothing is shared out between branches.

prompt: Three lamps are connected in parallel across a 3 V battery, each lamp on its own branch. What is the voltage across each lamp, in volts?
explain: Each branch is joined straight across the battery, so each lamp has the whole battery voltage across it, just as both voltmeters on the figure read the supply. Sharing the voltage belongs to series circuits; dividing by 3 would use that rule here. Each lamp has 3 V.

text: 5. Parallel: the currents add at a junction

alt: A wire carrying 0.50 A meets a junction and splits into two branches carrying 0.30 A and 0.20 A.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="p2spjn"><title id="p2spjn">A wire carrying 0.50 A meets a junction and splits into two branches carrying 0.30 A and 0.20 A</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><path d="M30 130 L170 130"/><path d="M170 70 L170 190"/><path d="M170 70 L370 70"/><path d="M170 190 L370 190"/></g><g fill="currentColor" stroke="none"><path d="M165.5 130 a4.5 4.5 0 1 0 9 0 a4.5 4.5 0 1 0 -9 0 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M106.5 130 L93.5 135.5 L93.5 124.5 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M296.5 70 L283.5 75.5 L283.5 64.5 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M296.5 190 L283.5 195.5 L283.5 184.5 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor"><text x="100" y="114" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15">0.50 A</text><text x="290" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15">0.30 A</text><text x="290" y="220" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15">0.20 A</text><text x="158" y="160" text-anchor="end" font-size="15">junction</text><text x="200" y="245" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" font-weight="600">0.30 A + 0.20 A = 0.50 A</text></g></svg>
caption: What flows into a junction flows out of it: the branch currents add up to the main-line current.

md: At a junction the charge divides between the branches, but none of it is lost and none is stored. What flows in equals what flows out. So **in parallel, the current in the main line is the sum of the branch currents**, and where the branches meet again their currents add back together.

**Read the figure.** 0.50 A arrives at the junction; 0.30 A takes the upper branch and 0.20 A the lower. Add the branches: 0.30 + 0.20 = 0.50 A. So a missing branch current is the main-line current take away the branches you know.

prompt: A current of 1.0 A flows into a junction and splits between two branches. One branch carries 0.6 A. What current flows in the other branch, in amps?
explain: A junction stores nothing, so the two branch currents must add back up to the 1.0 A that arrived, as the two branches on the figure add up to the main line. The other branch carries 1.0 − 0.6 = 0.4 A.

text: 6. See the current split and join

title: Current in parallel circuits
why: A three-minute lesson on what a parallel circuit is and how the current behaves as it splits into the branches and joins again.

title: Watch with your own paper in mind
md: The video is made for another exam board, and its circuits may be drawn a little differently. The rule it teaches is the one in section 5. If you hear **potential difference**, CCEA says **voltage**; the two mean the same, and on your paper you write voltage.

prompt: A current of 0.9 A reaches a junction and splits between two branches. Which statement is true?
options: the two branch currents add up to 0.9 A
some of the 0.9 A is used up at the junction
answer: the two branch currents add up to 0.9 A
explain: Charge is neither made nor lost at a junction: it only divides. So the currents leaving along the branches add up to the current that arrived, 0.9 A in all. Each branch carrying the full 0.9 A would need charge to be created, and a junction using some up would need it to vanish.

md: **The question.** A battery drives two equal resistors in parallel. A3 reads 0.30 A and V3 reads 4.5 V. Find A1, A2, V1 and V2.

**Step 1.** V2 is across a branch, so it reads the supply voltage, the same as V3: 4.5 V.
**Step 2.** V1 is across the battery itself: 4.5 V again.
**Step 3.** Equal resistors with equal voltages carry equal currents, so A2 = 0.30 A.
**Step 4.** A1 is in the main line, so it carries both: 0.30 + 0.30 = 0.60 A.

prompt: In the circuit shown, the battery is changed and ammeter A1 in the main line now reads 0.8 A. The two resistors are still equal. What does ammeter A2 on one branch read, in amps?
explain: A1 feeds both branches. Equal resistors with the same voltage across them take equal shares, so each branch carries half the main-line current, the way 0.60 A on the figure was two lots of 0.30 A. A2 reads 0.8 ÷ 2 = 0.4 A.

task: Build a battery with two light bulbs in parallel, one bulb on each branch. Put an ammeter in the main line and one on each branch and read all three: the main line should be the two branches added. Then remove one bulb and watch the other bulb and the main-line reading.

md: The bulb that is left shines exactly as before, because its branch still has the full battery voltage across it. The main-line reading drops to that one branch's current, because the charge now has one route instead of two. Both are the parallel rules of sections 4 and 5, seen happening.

prompt: Two identical lamps are connected in parallel across a battery. One lamp is unscrewed from its holder. What happens to the other lamp?
options: it stays as bright, because its branch still has the full battery voltage
it goes dimmer, because it now has to share the current
it goes out, because the circuit has been broken
answer: it stays as bright, because its branch still has the full battery voltage
explain: Each branch is its own route from one terminal of the battery to the other. Unscrewing one lamp breaks only that branch; the other branch still has the full battery voltage across it, so its lamp is exactly as bright. Only the main-line current falls.

caption: Four ammeters: two in the main line, either side of the branches, and one on each branch.

md: **Six meter readings, two given.** Summer 2019 Higher and Summer 2026 Foundation: two equal resistors in parallel, three ammeters, three voltmeters. First line: every voltmeter reads the supply; then the branches share the current equally.
**Ammeters either side of the branches.** Summer 2022, both tiers, as in the figure: A1 and A4 both carry the whole current; only A2 and A3 read a share.
**A resistor feeding an equal pair.** Summer 2021 Foundation gave one branch current in milliamps. The other branch matches it and the single resistor carries both. Convert to amps only for V = I R.

prompt: In the circuit shown, ammeter A1 reads 0.6 A and the two resistors are equal. What does ammeter A4 read?
explain: A4 is in the main line after the two branches have joined again, so it carries the whole current. The 0.3 A in each branch adds back to 0.6 A, exactly what A1 read before the split. Only the branch ammeters A2 and A3 read 0.3 A, and nothing in the circuit doubles a current.

caption: Two branches, the same voltage, different resistances: twice the resistance carries half the current.

md: Unequal branches do not split the current in half. Each branch still has the full supply voltage, so its current is that voltage divided by its own resistance, $I = V \div R$ (from V = I R). Twice the resistance takes half the current.
**Read the figure.** 10 Ω branch: 4.0 ÷ 10 = 0.40 A. 20 Ω branch: 4.0 ÷ 20 = 0.20 A. Main line: 0.40 + 0.20 = 0.60 A.

title: Where the Higher paper separates candidates
md: Summer 2023 Higher: nearly everyone could share a current between equal resistors; only the most able could when one resistance was double the other. Never halve unless the branches are equal.

prompt: A 4.5 V supply drives a 9 Ω resistor and an 18 Ω resistor connected in parallel. What current flows in the 18 Ω resistor, in amps?
explain: Each branch has the whole 4.5 V across it, so each takes the voltage divided by its own resistance, as the two branches on the figure did. The 18 Ω branch takes 4.5 ÷ 18 = 0.25 A; the 9 Ω branch takes twice as much, 0.50 A.

caption: No voltage given: the smaller resistance takes the larger share, and the shares add up to the total.

md: The Higher paper often gives only the current arriving at the branches, not the voltage (Summer 2021 and Summer 2023). The two branches still have the same voltage across them, so the smaller resistance takes the larger share. With one resistance twice the other, the currents are in the ratio 2 : 1, so split the total into three equal shares.
**Read the figure.** Step 1: one share is 0.90 ÷ 3 = 0.30 A. Step 2: the 20 Ω branch takes one share, 0.30 A. Step 3: the 10 Ω branch takes two shares, 0.60 A. Check: 0.60 + 0.30 = 0.90 A.

prompt: A current of 1.2 A arrives at a 20 Ω resistor and a 40 Ω resistor connected in parallel. What current flows in the 20 Ω resistor, in amps?
explain: Both resistors have the same voltage across them, so the 20 Ω one, with half the resistance, takes twice the current of the other. Split 1.2 A into three shares of 0.4 A: the 20 Ω resistor takes two shares, 0.8 A, and the other takes one, 0.4 A.

md:
Trace the route to tell series from parallel.
Series: one current everywhere; the voltages add up to the supply.
Parallel: the supply voltage on every branch; the branch currents add up to the main line.
Fill in a grid of missing meter readings, voltages first.
Share a current between unequal branches: twice the resistance, half the current.

These rules arrive as a circuit of ammeters and voltmeters, a mark for each missing reading, and then a V = I R calculation on the same circuit. Trace the route first; fill in every voltage, then the currents. The first mark is the reading that simply repeats; the last usually needs an addition, a subtraction or a milliamp conversion. Stuck? Ask which quantity is the same everywhere and which is shared.
